title: Microfinance Fundamentals
summary: Learn how microfinance works: providers and products, group and individual lending, the true cost of flat-rate loans, assessing repayment capacity, portfolio-at-risk and client protection in digital finance.
audience: Loan officers, cooperative members, NGO staff, finance students and small-business owners

body.p: Microfinance provides financial services (small loans, savings, insurance and payments) to people and small businesses who are poorly served by mainstream banks, often because they lack collateral, formal income records or nearby branches. Modern microfinance grew from pioneers such as Bangladesh's Grameen Bank in the 1970s and 1980s and now reaches many millions of clients worldwide, including across Africa.

list: Microfinance banks and deposit-taking institutions, licensed and supervised by central banks.
Non-bank microfinance institutions (MFIs) and NGOs, often credit-only.
Savings and credit cooperatives (SACCOs) owned by members.
Village savings and loan associations and rotating savings groups, informal but very widespread.
Mobile-money and digital lenders offering small, fast loans through phones.

body.p: Evidence shows microfinance helps many households manage cash flow, smooth spending and build businesses, but it is not a cure for poverty on its own, and over-indebtedness can harm borrowers. Good microfinance puts clients' wellbeing first.

body.tip: Savings services are as important as loans; safe ways to save help households cope with emergencies without borrowing.

body.p: Microfinance products are designed for small, irregular incomes and people without traditional collateral.

list: Group lending: small groups guarantee each other's loans; peer support and pressure replace collateral.
Individual loans: larger loans for established micro and small businesses, assessed on cash flow, sometimes with movable collateral.
Savings accounts and fixed deposits, including small, frequent deposits.
Microinsurance: low-cost cover for health, life, crops or livestock.
Agricultural loans timed to planting and harvest seasons.
Payments and remittances through agents and mobile money.

body.p: Clients often start with a small loan and receive larger loans after repaying on time. A trader might borrow R2000, then R4000 and later R8000 as her business and record grow. This progressive lending rewards good repayment and limits risk for the lender.

body.tip: Match loan size and repayment frequency to the business's real cash flow; weekly repayments suit daily traders, harvest-time repayments suit farmers.

lessons.title: Interest rates and the true cost of loans

body.p: Microloans are expensive to deliver: many small loans, frequent visits and higher risk. Interest rates are therefore higher than bank rates, but clients must be able to see the true cost and compare offers.

Consider a loan of 10 000 over 12 months at a flat rate of 2% a month. Flat interest is charged on the original amount every month: 10 000 x 0.02 x 12 = 2400. The client repays 12 400 in 12 instalments of about 1033.33.

But the client is repaying principal every month, so on average owes far less than 10 000. Calculated on the declining balance, the same payments correspond to about 3.48% a month, an annual percentage rate (APR) of about 41.7%, almost double the 24% that "2% a month" seems to suggest. Fees and compulsory savings can raise the effective cost further.

list: Responsible lenders disclose the APR or effective rate, total cost and all fees before signing.
Many regulators now require standard disclosure and some cap interest rates or fees.
Clients should compare total repayable amounts, not just headline rates.

body.tip: Always ask, "What is the total amount I will repay, including all fees?" and compare that figure across lenders.

body.p: Lenders assess whether a borrower can and will repay. A common framework is the five Cs: character (reputation and repayment history), capacity (cash flow to repay), capital (the borrower's own investment), collateral (assets that can secure the loan) and conditions (the business environment and loan purpose).

Loan officers analyse household and business cash flow together, because in small businesses they are mixed. If a trader's monthly income is 8000 and essential household and business expenses are 5500, the surplus is 2500. A prudent lender might limit instalments to about half the surplus, 1250 a month, leaving a buffer for bad months.

list: Visit the business and home, check records, and talk to suppliers or neighbours.
Check credit bureau reports where available, to avoid lending to people already over-indebted.
Ask about other loans, including informal ones.
Use alternative data carefully, such as mobile-money transaction history, with the client's consent.

body.tip: Lend for productive purposes the borrower understands, and never pressure clients to borrow more than they need.

body.p: A microfinance institution's main asset is its loan portfolio. Monitoring its quality is essential to survival.

Portfolio at risk over 30 days (PAR30) is the outstanding balance of all loans with a payment more than 30 days late, divided by the total outstanding portfolio. If loans with 150 000 outstanding are over 30 days late in a portfolio of 2 000 000, PAR30 = 7.5%. Many institutions aim to keep PAR30 below about 5%.

list: Follow up missed payments within days, respectfully and consistently.
Understand the reason: illness, business failure or wilful default each need a different response.
Reschedule loans for genuine hardship rather than pushing clients into new debt.
Write off loans that will not be recovered, and provide for expected losses in the accounts.
Diversify across sectors and areas so one shock (such as drought) does not hit everything.

body.tip: Rising PAR is an early warning; investigate the branch, product or loan officer where it is concentrated.

body.p: Microfinance serves people who may have limited financial experience and few alternatives, so client protection matters. Widely used principles include appropriate product design, preventing over-indebtedness, transparency, responsible pricing, fair and respectful treatment, privacy of client data and mechanisms for complaints.

Mobile and app-based lenders offer instant small loans using phone and transaction data. They bring convenience and reach, but also risks: very short loan terms with high effective costs, repeated borrowing, aggressive debt collection and misuse of phone contacts and personal data. Several countries have introduced licensing and conduct rules for digital lenders.

list: Read terms and the total repayment before accepting a digital loan.
Check that the lender is licensed with the relevant regulator.
Avoid borrowing from one lender to repay another.
Report abusive collection practices to the regulator.

body.p: Financial education, such as budgeting and understanding loan costs, makes all microfinance products work better for clients.

body.tip: For a business, a loan should earn more than it costs. If 100 extra sales a month at a profit of 20 each would only produce 2000 against a 1033 instalment, check that the sales are realistic before borrowing.
